context.text: In August 1917, between the fall of the tsar and the Bolshevik coup, the Russian Church's great council met in Moscow and restored the patriarchate abolished by Peter the Great, electing Tikhon of Moscow. Within weeks the new Soviet state had begun the war against it.

narrative.text: Decrees separated church and state and stripped the Church of legal personality and property; the murder of clergy began in 1918, Metropolitan Vladimir of Kiev the protomartyr of the episcopate, and swelled with campaigns to seize church valuables, the state-sponsored 'Renovationist' schism, and waves of arrests. Under Stalin the assault became annihilation: by 1939 only a few hundred churches functioned in the USSR and nearly the whole episcopate had been shot or sent to the camps. Solovki monastery, turned prison camp, held so many clergy it was called the 'cathedral of the new martyrs.'

A wartime reprieve allowed the patriarchate's restoration in 1943, but Khrushchev renewed the persecution, and after 1945 the same pattern, confiscation, infiltration, imprisonment, was imposed across Orthodox Eastern Europe. Through it all the Church endured: babushki kept the parishes alive, the faithful baptized in secret, and in 1988 the millennium of the Baptism of Rus was celebrated openly as the system entered collapse. The council of 2000 glorified over a thousand new martyrs and confessors by name; the tally has grown since.

significance.text: The communist persecution exceeded, in scale, every persecution of the ancient world combined, and gave the Church its largest company of martyrs. Orthodoxy's twentieth century, its emigrations, jurisdictions abroad, and theological renaissance in exile, is unintelligible without it.

uncertainty: Exact victim counts remain debated and archival work continues; responsible estimates for executed Orthodox clergy alone run to the tens of thousands, with the persecution's total toll far higher. This entry gives the settled outline, not disputed figures.
